d.title: An array is one buffer and three facts about how to read it
d.caption: A Python list of numbers is a list of **pointers** to separate integer objects scattered across the heap. An array is a single block of raw bytes with no per-element object at all — and `strides`, the number of bytes to step per axis, is the piece that makes a view possible.

d.title: Four ways to compute a * b + 1 on a million elements
d.caption: Measured. The gap is 200×, not 10%, because vectorising removes the work rather than reducing it: one dispatch instead of a million, no int or float object per element, and a contiguous C loop the compiler can unroll into SIMD registers. `np.vectorize` is in this list because its name promises otherwise — the documentation calls it a convenience, not a performance tool.

d.title: The shape mismatch that returns a plausible number
d.caption: Shapes align from the **right**, and two lengths are compatible when they are equal or when one is 1. The dangerous case is the last pair: `(4,)` against `(4,1)` broadcasts to a 4×4 matrix of every pairwise difference, and `.mean()` on it returns a small believable float. On 500 rows it misreports your RMSE for months; on 50,000 it is a 20 GB allocation. Assert shape equality inside every metric you write.
cells: the None makes it a column

d.title: One question decides view or copy: is the selection evenly spaced
d.caption: If what you asked for can be described by a start, a stop and a step, you get a view over the existing bytes. If it cannot, a new array has to be built. The last row is the exception worth memorising: `a[mask] = 0` is `__setitem__`, not indexing-then-assigning, so it writes to the original even though reading `a[mask]` would have copied.

d.title: axis is the dimension that disappears
d.caption: Reducing a `(3, 4)` array along axis 0 gives `(4,)`: the axis named is the one removed. `keepdims=True` leaves it behind as length 1 so the result still broadcasts against the source — which is what makes row normalisation a one-liner instead of a reshape.

d.title: Two random APIs, and why the old one is not a style choice
d.caption: The legacy functions share **one global state with every piece of code in the process**. Any library that calls `np.random.*` advances it, so what your next call returns depends on what else ran first — which is a reproducibility bug that only appears when you add a dependency.

d.title: Two operations wearing six names
d.caption: There are only two ideas here — lengthen an existing axis, or add a new one. The trouble is that three of the names change meaning between 1-D and 2-D input, so the same call does two different things depending on what you hand it.

d.title: Sorting the values, and sorting the positions
d.caption: `argsort` is the form that generalises: indices can be applied to any array of the same length, which is how a feature matrix and its labels stay together through a sort. The lexsort row is the one that costs people an afternoon — the **last** key in the tuple is the primary one.

d.title: Five products, and which one you meant
d.caption: `a * b` on two (3,3) arrays gives nine independent products, not a matrix product. `np.dot` is the one to avoid in new code: it is the inner product on 1-D, the matrix product on 2-D, and something else again on higher dimensions.

d.title: A compound dtype describes one record's layout
d.caption: A structured array is a row type: the fields of one record sit next to each other in memory. That is why `a["age"]` is a **strided** view rather than a contiguous one — the other fields sit between consecutive values, which is the opposite of how a DataFrame stores a column.

d.title: Counting temporaries, not lines
d.caption: `(a * b + c) / d` looks like one expression and allocates three full-size arrays. This matters only at the scale where it matters — optimising a 10 MB calculation is wasted effort — but knowing the rule is what lets you recognise the problem when the array is 10 GB.

d.title: Three ways to compute a moving average
d.caption: A moving average slides weights along an array and takes a weighted sum, which is convolution. The `mode` argument is where the quiet error lives: `"same"` pads with zeros, so the first and last values are dragged towards zero — an artefact that looks like a trend.
